title: SpaceX Stock Hits Record Low After Seven Straight Days of Losses
excerpt: Shares have plunged 47% from their all-time high as Meta Platforms overtakes the rocket and AI company in market value.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX shares fell 3.3% to $119.85, marking a record low after seven days of losses.
  • The stock has dropped 47% from its peak, erasing $1.09 trillion in market value.
  • Meta Platforms now surpasses SpaceX in market cap, valued at $1.64 trillion.
  • Operational setbacks, including scrubbed launches, are increasing investor anxiety ahead of earnings report.

  • SpaceX shares fell 3.3% to $119.85 on Monday, marking a seventh consecutive day of losses and a new record closing low since the company's June IPO.
  • The stock has plunged 47% from its all-time high of $225.64, erasing roughly $1.09 trillion in market value and dropping SpaceX to eighth place among U.S. companies.
  • Meta Platforms has overtaken SpaceX in market capitalization, with Meta at $1.64 trillion versus SpaceX's $1.59 trillion.
  • A scrubbed Falcon 9 launch on Monday and an aborted Starship test last Thursday have compounded investor anxiety ahead of SpaceX's first-ever earnings report, expected in August.

SpaceX shares closed at $119.85 on Monday, down 3.3% on the day and marking a seventh consecutive session of losses for what was once the most hotly anticipated IPO of the decade. The stock has now shed 47% from its all-time high above $225, set just days after the company began trading in mid-June following a record $86 billion offering at $135 per share.

The seven-day losing streak has wiped out roughly $1.09 trillion in market capitalization, according to Dow Jones Market Data. SpaceX's market cap now stands at approximately $1.59 trillion, pushing it below Meta Platforms for the first time. Meta, riding a strong July that has seen its stock rise nearly 15%, commands a market value of $1.64 trillion.

Setbacks Mount for Musk's Space Empire

The slide has been fueled by a series of operational setbacks. On Monday morning, SpaceX scrubbed a Falcon 9 launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California that was scheduled to carry 24 satellites into orbit. The company said the vehicle and its payload "remain safe," but offered no timeline for a reattempt.

Last Thursday, SpaceX was forced to abort the 12th test flight of its Starship mega-rocket after some booster engines failed to ignite, triggering an automatic shutdown. CEO Elon Musk said two engines need to be replaced. The company initially targeted a relaunch as early as Monday, but has since pushed its 13th Starship test to no sooner than Thursday — the day after Musk is scheduled to lead Tesla's second-quarter earnings call.

"Starship drives the connectivity pillar and the AI pillar. Any push-out or delay really delays the growth story."

— Greg Pendy, Clear Street Research

Short Sellers Circle as Lock-Up Looms

Technical factors have amplified the selling pressure. About 110 million shares of SpaceX have been borrowed and sold short, according to FactSet — a small fraction of total shares outstanding but roughly 17% of the limited float available for trading since the IPO.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=iyMhmD3jsIo

Two catalysts loom. SpaceX's inaugural earnings report as a public company is expected in August, though no date has been set. More critically, the first of several lock-up expirations will free up approximately 911.5 million shares for sale by employees and early investors on the second trading day following that report.

Operational Setbacks Impacting SpaceX
›Falcon 9 launch scrubbed on Monday.
›Starship test aborted due to engine failure.
›First earnings report expected in August.
›Lock-up expiration could release 911.5 million shares.

"Investors are becoming more cognizant that much of SpaceX is about its xAI ambitions," said Dec Mullarkey, managing director at SLC Management. "As markets get more cautious on the cost and efficacy of the intensive buildout, SpaceX plans may sound too far removed from immediate cash flow."

Broader Ripple Effects

SpaceX's struggles are reverberating beyond its own stock. The company's weak post-IPO performance is reportedly giving other AI-focused companies contemplating public offerings cold feet, particularly as more recent IPOs have received lukewarm receptions.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DanpjeugJz6/

The company — which houses rocket-launch, satellite-internet and artificial-intelligence businesses following its merger with Musk's xAI earlier this year — has signed computing deals with Anthropic, Google and startup Reflection AI that could generate tens of billions in annual revenue when fully ramped. On Friday, the Wall Street Journal reported SpaceX was in talks with the Pentagon about additional AI computing capacity at its Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee.

What's Next

For Indian-origin investors who flocked to SpaceX during its record-breaking IPO, the stock's trajectory has been a harsh lesson in the risks of newly public companies with sky-high valuations. SpaceX was valued at roughly 45 times estimated 2026 sales at its peak, a multiple that left little room for the kind of execution stumbles that have since materialized.

SpaceX's Starship test on Thursday will be closely watched. If successful, it could help stabilize sentiment around a rocket program that analysts say is central to the company's long-term value proposition, including plans for orbital AI data centers powered by solar energy. If not, the selling may have further to run.
